questions.q: The Court's Certified climate cell calls one of Rioja's three subzones the coolest and wettest. Name it.
questions.exp: Rioja Alavesa, in the Basque province of Álava, sits on high terraces beneath the Sierra de Cantabria and takes the most Atlantic influence. The Court calls Rioja Alta continental and Rioja Oriental, the former Rioja Baja, Mediterranean: lower, hotter and drier, where Garnacha ripens best.

questions.q: Beside calcareous clay and alluvial ground, which third soil does the Court list for Rioja?
questions.exp: The Court's three Rioja soils are calcareous clay, ferrous clay and alluvial. Pale calcareous clay covers Alavesa's terraces and the higher Alta and is the soil the finest Tempranillo prefers; reddish, iron-rich clay patches the Alta and the Oriental, and alluvial gravel lines the Ebro and its tributaries.

questions.q: Which ageing term does the Court give a Rioja Tinto that must age at least three years, one of them in oak?
questions.exp: The Court's ladder for Rioja Tinto is Crianza at two years with one in oak, Reserva at three years with one in oak, and Gran Reserva at five years with two in oak. The Consejo's current rules add at least six months in bottle for a Reserva, and its burgundy back label shows the tier at a glance.

questions.q: Some modern Rioja producers make fruit-focused wines and leave Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva off the label. Which cask wood does the Court say they favour?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified style cell sets modern producers using French oak and avoiding the traditional ageing terms against the classic houses, whose long ageing in American oak gives coconut, vanilla and dill. A modern wine is usually named for its vineyard or its estate rather than for its time in cask.

questions.q: Bordeaux merchants who came to Rioja when phylloxera ruined their own vineyards brought a standard barrel with them. What is its capacity?
accept: two hundred and twenty five litres
questions.exp: The Court asks for the link between Bordeaux and Rioja during phylloxera's devastation of France. Merchants who crossed the Pyrenees brought the 225 litre barrica and Bordeaux's habit of long cask ageing, which the Haro and Logroño houses kept, choosing American oak; Spanish law still counts only casks of 330 litres or less towards the ageing terms.

questions.q: Which of these houses stands on the Court's list of Rioja producers?
questions.exp: The Court's Rioja houses are Marqués de Riscal, Marqués de Cáceres, Finca Allende, Bodegas López de Heredia and La Rioja Alta. Vega Sicilia is the Court's Ribera del Duero estate, Clos Mogador one of its Priorat names and Pazo Señorans one of its Rías Baixas Albariño houses.

questions.q: A traditional Rioja Gran Reserva has spent years in American oak and taken on a mellow, oxidative, savoury character. Which dish suits it best?
questions.exp: The Court asks how oak and oxidation change a pairing. Long ageing softens a Gran Reserva's tannin and adds leather, dried fruit and vanilla, which meet roast lamb, game or aged cheese; the same notes swamp raw shellfish, clash with the chilli and lime of a papaya salad, and taste thin against a sweet dessert.
